title: Foundation: the MapleHelper combo helper and the game data reader
tagline: The combo helper gamelab grew from, its reused key engine, and the game's data files
summary: `maplehelper` is the original one-button combo helper: a keyboard hook, a controller, a combo engine, four escape combos and an on-screen coach, plus measured game facts, an OCR reader for the HUD and pickup messages, and human-like mouse trails. gamelab still runs on its pieces: its key names, Win32 input, config loader, combo engine and moves, game facts and OCR. `gamedata` reads the game's own .wz and .ms data files, which gamelab's maps, physics, sprites and HUD readers are built from.
details_md:
### Two packages under the autonomous player

**maplehelper** started on 2026-10-18 as a helper for a person playing a dart thief: press F1-F4 and it plays a timed
escape combo (Jump-Throw, Back Off & Throw, Hop Back & Throw, Jump-Back Shot) while a click-through overlay narrates
each step so she can learn it. Its runtime is small and pure standard library (ctypes + tkinter):

```
key press -> hook.KeyboardHook (WH_KEYBOARD_LL thread) -> controller.Controller.on_key
          -> engine.Runner.trigger -> combo-runner thread: combos.<combo>(Ctx) -> win32.send_key (SendInput, scan code)
                                                                             -> app.Narrator -> coach.Coach (Tk, main thread)
```

gamelab began as the way to measure those combos in the game, and grew into the autonomous hunter. It kept the
helper's foundations instead of rewriting them:

| gamelab uses | from here | for |
|---|---|---|
| `keys.Key`, `parse`, `KEY_CODES` | `maplehelper/keys.py` | every key name; the player's list of pressable keys |
| `send_key`, `send_mouse_move`, `send_mouse_button`, `foreground_title`, `precise_timers` | `maplehelper/win32.py` | the elevated key player's presses and clicks, the cursor trail, the focus check |
| `config.load`, `GameKeys`, `Timing`, `Character`, `characters()` | `maplehelper/config.py` | her keys, timing and stats from `config.toml`; who plays |
| `engine.Ctx`, `_Silent`, `LEFT`/`RIGHT`, `combos.COMBOS` | `maplehelper/engine.py`, `combos.py` | `control/timeline.py` plays the combos on a virtual clock into exact key timelines; LEFT/RIGHT across the stack |
| `actions.ACTIONS` | `maplehelper/actions.py` | `gamelab do <move>` |
| `game.COMBAT`, `MOVEMENT` | `maplehelper/game.py` | the 730 ms attack lock, 530 ms release, tap-turn and slide times |
| `ocr.shared`, `LOOT`, `parse_loot`, `match_prefix`, `ITEM_NAMES`, `EXP_TO_NEXT` | `maplehelper/ocr/` | the pickup log, chat line, stat window, looting, EXP gains |
| `mouse_trail.generate_trail` | `maplehelper/mouse_trail.py` | the player's human-like pointer moves (the Lie Detector's mouse mini-game) |

Because combos and moves are plain functions of a `Ctx`, the same script can be played by the helper's runner,
timed by a dry run, or recorded by gamelab's virtual clock, so tests play exactly what the helper plays.

**gamedata** (also 2026-10-18) reads a *copy* of the game's `appdata\Data` folder: the classic Wizet `.wz` packages
(text only XOR-masked; directory offsets scrambled by a client-version hash found by trial) and the newer `.ms` packs
(ChaCha20 with keys from the file name and a stored salt; Mob and Skill data). `canvas.py` decodes pictures and knows
where newer clients keep the pixels; `tables.py` summarizes items, monsters, maps, skills, physics and animation
delays as JSON. gamelab's `localization/mapdata.py` builds its map model (platforms, ropes, portals, spawns,
`Physics.img`) from it, `perception` matches monster sprites, item icons and HUD glyphs taken from it, and the
simulator's monsters use its stats.

### Measured, not guessed

Most numbers here were measured in the game: the attack lock (730 ms), star release (530 ms), the Jump-Back Shot's
held arrows (160/160 against ~6% failures with taps), running jumps keyed no sooner than 150 ms after the arrow. Where
the game data holds a number, gamedata reads it instead (walk speed from `Physics.img`, monster speeds, skill MP). The
EXP table and item names come from a fan database because the data files don't hold them (item names were checked
against String.wz).

### Limits

Both packages sit at the bottom of the stack: neither imports anything of gamelab, and `gamedata` imports nothing of `maplehelper` (a commit of 2026-10-20 notes "maplehelper can't import gamelab", so a number gamelab measured, like `RUN_JUMP_AFTER_MS`, is copied here with where it comes from). The elevated key player must not load `gamedata` or `tkinter` (tests/test_architecture.py checks it loads none of either), so the coach overlay and the data readers stay out of it. The combo
helper and its README predate gamelab: its pixel distances are 1920x1080 window pixels, while gamelab plans in map
units. Nothing under `gamedata/data` is committed: a fresh checkout needs `python -m gamedata copy` first.

modules.title: maplehelper package init
modules.tagline: Pins numpy's BLAS to one thread before anything imports numpy
modules.summary: The package's whole body is one environment setting: `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1` unless already set. Every `from maplehelper... import` runs this file first, so the helper, its OCR try-out and anything else that imports maplehelper before numpy get it; `gamelab/__init__.py` carries the same line for gamelab's own processes.
modules.details_md:
The docstring names the package: *one-button escape combos with an on-screen coach for a dart thief*.

The only code is `os.environ.setdefault("OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS", "1")`. OpenBLAS (numpy's linear-algebra library, from
`environment.yml`) commits a work buffer per thread as soon as numpy loads. On this PC's 24 threads that came to about
**3 GB of commit charge per Python process**, and on 2026-10-24 a few such processes ran the machine out of commit
charge. Nothing in the stack needs threaded BLAS, so one thread is enough (18 MB instead of 3 GB).

It must run *before* numpy is first imported, which is why it sits in the package's `__init__`: any import of a
maplehelper module runs it first. `gamelab/__init__.py` has the very same line (and comment) for gamelab's processes,
and the conda env's `sitecustomize.py` sets it too, as a further line of defence; `setdefault` means an explicit
value in the environment still wins.

modules.title: The helper app (wiring)
modules.tagline: Loads config, then starts the keyboard hook, combo runner and coach overlay
modules.summary: `main` is the combo helper's whole life cycle. It loads and validates `config.toml`, optionally swaps in the key bindings gamelab last read off the game, and wires a `KeyboardHook` to a `Controller` to a `Runner` that presses keys with `win32.send_key` and narrates on the `Coach` overlay. The Tk overlay owns the main thread until Ctrl+C.
modules.details_md:
### Start-up order

1. **Arguments.** `--config` (default `DEFAULT_CONFIG`, the repo's `config.toml`), `--debug` (log every key press with
   the focused window's title) and `--config-keys` (use `config.toml`'s `[keys]` as written).
2. **Config.** `config.load(path, combo names)`. A `ConfigError` prints `Config problem: ...` and returns 2.
3. **Her keys as the game has them.** Unless `--config-keys`, `config.followed(cfg, <config dir>/gamelab/lab/keybindings-thief.json)`
   replaces `[keys]` with the bindings gamelab last read off the game's KEY BINDINGS window (when that file exists,
   binds her arrows, jump and attack to known key names, isn't marked doubted, and puts no game key on a combo button or the slow-mode key). The returned note is printed in the banner.
4. **Logging through a queue** (`_start_logging`): log records go into a `SimpleQueue` and a `QueueListener` thread
   prints them. The comment says why: printing straight from the keyboard hook could stall (for example while text is
   selected in the console), and **Windows silently removes low-level hooks that stall**.
5. `win32.enable_dpi_awareness()`, then build `Coach()`, `Runner(win32.send_key, cfg.keys, cfg.timing,
   Narrator(coach), COMBOS)` and `KeyboardHook(Controller(cfg, runner, win32.foreground_title).on_key)`.
6. Ctrl+C is routed to `coach.request_quit()` (a flag, so it's safe from a signal handler).
7. Inside `win32.precise_timers()` (1 ms timer resolution instead of ~15 ms): start the runner thread, start the hook
   thread, print the banner (each hotkey with its combo's title, the abort and slow-mode keys), then `coach.run()`
   blocks in Tk's main loop. On the way out it stops the hook, the runner and the log listener.

### Narrator

`Narrator` is the `Display` the runner talks to. It logs each step as `title | text` and forwards it to the coach:
`step` for a new step, `done` for the ending plus the whole recipe and how long to linger.

### Threads

Main thread: Tk. `keyboard-hook`: the low-level hook's message loop. `combo-runner`: plays combos. Plus the logging
listener. Nothing here blocks the hook.

modules.title: Keyboard hook
modules.tagline: A system-wide low-level keyboard hook that can hide keys from the game
modules.summary: `KeyboardHook` installs a Windows `WH_KEYBOARD_LL` hook on its own thread and calls `on_key(vk, is_down)` for every real key event. Returning True swallows the event so the game never sees it. Events the helper injected itself are recognized by their `INJECTED_TAG` and skipped.
modules.details_md:
A *low-level keyboard hook* is a callback Windows calls for every key event on the desktop, before any
window gets it. This one lives on a dedicated daemon thread named `keyboard-hook`:

- `_run` records its thread id, calls `SetWindowsHookExW(WH_KEYBOARD_LL, ...)` and then sits in a
  `GetMessageW` loop. Windows delivers the hook callback *while this thread waits for messages*, so the loop body is
  empty. When the loop ends the hook is removed with `UnhookWindowsHookEx`.
- `start` launches the thread and waits on a `threading.Event` until the hook is installed; if `SetWindowsHookExW`
  failed, the `OSError` is re-raised on the caller's thread.
- `stop` posts `WM_QUIT` to the hook thread (`PostThreadMessageW`) and joins it with a 2 s timeout.

### The callback

`_callback(n_code, w_param, l_param)` only acts on `HC_ACTION`. It reads the `KBDLLHOOKSTRUCT` (Windows' record of
the event: key code, scan code, flags, time and `dwExtraInfo`, a free number the sender of an injected event may
set) and **skips events whose `dwExtraInfo` equals `win32.INJECTED_TAG`** (`0x4D484C50`, "MHLP"): those are the helper's own key presses,
sent by `win32.send_key`, and must not trigger combos. For the rest, key down is `WM_KEYDOWN` or `WM_SYSKEYDOWN`
(Alt combinations arrive as the SYS variants). If `on_key` returns True the callback returns 1, which hides the event
from every other program; otherwise it passes it on with `CallNextHookEx`.

Any exception in `on_key` is printed and swallowed ("never let a bug here break her keyboard").

### Why it's built so

Windows silently removes a low-level hook whose callback is too slow. So `on_key` must return quickly: the controller
only looks things up and hands work to the runner's thread, and logging goes through a queue (`app._start_logging`).
The ctypes callback object (`win32.HOOKPROC(self._callback)`) is kept on `self._proc`: the code's comment says it
must stay referenced while the hook is installed.

modules.title: Controller (what a key press means)
modules.tagline: Decides per real key press: run a combo, stop, slow mode, facing, or pass through
modules.summary: `Controller.on_key` runs inside the keyboard hook for every real key. While the game window is in front it maps combo hotkeys to `Runner.trigger`, the abort key to `Runner.abort`, the slow-mode key to `Runner.toggle_slow`, and her arrow presses to `Runner.note_facing`. Combo and slow-mode buttons are hidden from the game; everything else passes through.
modules.details_md:
Built from the `Config`: a map of hotkey virtual-key code to combo name, her left and right arrows, the
abort key and the slow-mode key.

### Per key event

- **Key up.** If the key is one the controller swallowed on its way down (kept in `_held`), the up is swallowed too
  and forgotten, so the game never sees an up without its down. Other ups pass through.
- **Key down of a held button** (keyboard auto-repeat while she keeps it pressed) is swallowed and does nothing.
- **Focus check.** `win32.foreground_title()` must contain `game_window_title` (default `"MapleStory"`); otherwise
  the key passes through untouched. With `--debug` every key down is logged with the focused title.
- **Left / right arrow** → `runner.note_facing(LEFT/RIGHT)`, and the arrow still reaches the game. The runner uses
  her last turn to decide which way is "away" for the next combo.
- **Abort** (default Esc) → `runner.abort()`; Esc still reaches the game (config.toml: "Esc still reaches the game
  too").
- **Slow mode** (default F12) → swallowed, remembered in `_held`, `runner.toggle_slow()`.
- **A combo hotkey** (default F1-F4) → swallowed, remembered, `runner.trigger(name)`. The result is logged when it
  is `QUEUED` ("runs when the current combo ends") or `DROPPED` ("pressed too early in the current combo").

### Why

The controller only reads a dict and calls the runner, which hands work to its own thread, so the hook returns at
once. Swallowing the hotkeys is what lets F1-F4 be combo buttons without the game also acting on them; `config.py`
refuses a hotkey that is also one of her game keys for the same reason.

modules.title: Combo engine (Runner and Ctx)
modules.tagline: Plays combo scripts with timed key presses; abortable, narrated, reused by gamelab
modules.summary: `Runner` plays one combo at a time on its own thread so the keyboard hook never waits; it queues a press made in a combo's last 300 ms and drops earlier ones. A combo is a plain function of a `Ctx`, whose `down`, `up`, `tap` and `wait` press keys and sleep, and which raises `Aborted` the moment Esc is hit. gamelab reuses `Ctx` with a virtual clock (`control/timeline.py`) to turn the same scripts into exact key timelines.
modules.details_md:
### Ctx: what a combo script acts through

`Ctx` is built per run with the key sender, her `GameKeys`, the `Timing`, her facing, slow mode, an abort `Event`, a
`Display` and the combo's title.

- `front` is the arrow pointing at the monsters (the way she faced when she pressed the button) and `back` the other;
  both are fixed for the whole combo. `facing` and `turned_at` (a `perf_counter_ns`) update as the script presses arrows.
- `down(key)` checks the abort flag, sends the key down and remembers it as held; `up(key)` always sends the release
  (never aborts, so keys can always be let go).
- `wait(ms)` is `abort.wait(ms / 1000)`: it returns early and raises `Aborted` the instant the flag is set, so Esc
  stops a combo mid-wait, not at the next step.
- `tap(key, ms=None)` = down, wait (`key_press`, 40 ms, by default), up.
- `say(text, pause=True)` appends to the recipe and shows the step; in slow mode it then waits `slow_pause` (900 ms),
  except for mid-move steps marked `pause=False`.
- Helpers: `jump_attack` (jump, `air_delay` 60 ms, attack: an attack in the air throws a star instead of swiping the
  claw), `air_throw` (Lucky Seven if bound, else attack), `throw(times)` (Lucky Seven, or a jump attack when Lucky
  Seven isn't bound, each followed by `throw_gap`, 750 ms) and the labels used in coach text.

### Runner: one combo at a time

`trigger(name)` never blocks. Under a lock:
- idle → mark busy, clear abort, put the combo on a `SimpleQueue` → `STARTED`;
- busy and the running combo's expected end is more than `buffer_window` (300 ms) away → `DROPPED`;
- busy and within the last 300 ms → keep it as `_buffered` (a newer press replaces an older one) → `QUEUED`.

The `combo-runner` thread (`_work`) takes combos off the queue. `_run` first sends key-up for both arrows ("start
clean even if she's holding an arrow"), works out the combo's length with a **dry run** (`expected_ms`: `_DryRun` is a
`Ctx` whose sender does nothing and whose `wait` just adds up milliseconds) to set `_ends_at`, then runs the script.
The ending is "Done ✓", "Stopped" (on `Aborted`) or "Error, see console". `finally` releases every held key, settles
her facing and shows the recipe for `recap` (3000 ms).

**Facing**: whoever turned her last wins. If the combo's last arrow press (`ctx.turned_at`) is later than her own
(`_her_turn_at`, set by `note_facing`), the runner takes the combo's facing; otherwise hers stands.

After a combo `_work` checks `_buffered`: if set, it clears the abort flag *under the lock* (so an Esc arriving from
then on still stops the buffered combo) and queues it; otherwise the runner goes idle. `abort()` sets the flag and
forgets any buffered press.

### Why it's built so

The hook must return quickly, so all sleeping happens on the runner's thread. Waiting on an `Event` instead of
`time.sleep` makes aborts instant. Combos as plain functions of a `Ctx` let other code play them differently:
`_DryRun` times them, gamelab's `control/timeline.py` subclasses `Ctx` as `_Clock` (sender records `[ms, key, down/up]`,
`wait` advances a virtual clock, `_Silent` display) so tests and the in-game key player play exactly what the helper
plays, and `maplehelper/actions.py`'s moves run on the same `Ctx`.

modules.title: The combos
modules.tagline: Four escape combos for a dart thief, written as step-by-step scripts
modules.summary: Jump-Throw, Back Off & Throw, Hop Back & Throw and Jump-Back Shot, each a function of a `Ctx` with a narrated `say` per step. `COMBOS` lists them with the names config.toml's `[hotkeys]` use. gamelab plays the very same scripts in the game (`gamelab combo`) and in tests through `control/timeline.py`.
modules.details_md:
Each combo is a few lines of `Ctx` calls. "Front" is the way she faced when the button was pressed (toward the
monsters), "back" away from them. Timings are `config.toml [timing]`'s (defaults in `config.Timing`).

| Combo (`[hotkeys]` name, default key) | Steps |
|---|---|
| Jump-Throw (`jump_throw`, F1) | jump, `air_delay` (60 ms), attack in mid-air so a star is thrown, then `throw_gap` (750 ms) so it ends when she can act again |
| Back Off & Throw (`back_off`, F2) | hold back `walk_away` (500 ms), tap front `turn_tap` (50 ms) to turn without walking far, throw ×2 |
| Hop Back & Throw (`hop_back`, F3) | a Jump-Back Shot, then one more throw |
| Jump-Back Shot (`jump_back_shot`, F4) | hold back; after `run_up` (100 ms) tap jump; keep pushing away for `air_delay` (60 ms); release back; hold front for `turn_lead` (50 ms) and **keep it held** through the air throw; release; `throw_gap` |

The Jump-Back Shot's star comes out as she lands. The run-up matters ("already moving when she jumps, so the jump
carries her away"; shorter sometimes gives a straight-up jump), and the turn arrow is held, not tapped, because right
after takeoff the game sometimes ignores a turn.

**Slow mode rule** (module docstring): `say` pauses in slow mode, so a pausing step must start a complete move, never
mid-jump. The two in-air steps of the Jump-Back Shot are `pause=False`.

**Why these timings.** In-game measurements (2026-10-18): a regular attack's star leaves ~530 ms after the key and the
game ignores jump and attack presses until ~730 ms after it, so `key_press + throw_gap` (40 + 750) must clear 730.
At the old `throw_gap` of 650, queued Jump-Back Shots jumped only 2 of 6 times and F2/F3's second throw was always
ignored. Quick taps in the Jump-Back Shot jumped straight up or threw the wrong way in about 6% of shots; the held
pattern went 160 for 160.

**Adding a combo**: write a function, add it to `COMBOS`, give it a button in `[hotkeys]` (README). config.load
refuses a `[hotkeys]` entry that names no combo, so `COMBOS` is also what gamelab passes to `config.load`.

modules.title: Reusable moves
modules.tagline: Walk, jump, climb, loot, attack and drink as Ctx moves built on measured numbers
modules.summary: Each move takes a combo `Ctx`, so the helper's runner and gamelab can both play it under the same timing rules. Distances are game-window pixels at 1920x1080, turned into key-hold times with `game.MOVEMENT`. `ACTIONS` maps names to functions and argument converters for `gamelab do <move> ...`.
modules.details_md:
### The moves

- `walk(c, direction, px)`: hold the arrow `walk_ms(px)` then wait `stop_slide_ms` (200 ms) for her slide.
  `walk_ms(px) = max(tap_turn_ms, round((px - walk_start_px) / walk_px_per_ms))`, from the measured line "holding an
  arrow for t ms moves her about 12 + 0.209 t px".
- `turn(c, direction)`: a 50 ms arrow tap (turns or stands her up without walking), then `reaction_ms` (100 ms).
- `jump(c, direction=None)`: in place (~104 px up), or a running jump: arrow down, wait
  `max(reaction_ms, RUN_JUMP_AFTER_MS)` = 150 ms, tap jump, wait `jump_airtime_ms` (530), release, wait 100.
- `jump_to_ledge(c, direction, ledge_px, height_px, own_edge_px)`: land on a higher ledge. Refuses (ValueError) a
  ledge within 5 px of the jump's 104 px peak, one farther than 0.85 × `ledge_takeoff_px(height)` from the take-off
  point (her own edge less `EDGE_MARGIN_PX`, 15 px), and a take-off with less than 150 ms of run-up (~31 px) before
  her own edge ("step back first"). Then one continuous run: arrow down, jump keyed so she leaves at the take-off point
  (never sooner than 150 ms), hold through the airtime.
- `ledge_takeoff_px(h)`: platforms can be jumped through from below, so she only needs to still be `h` up when she
  reaches the edge. With a parabola peaking at `jump_height_px` after `jump_peak_ms`, the last moment she is that high
  is `peak_ms × (1 + sqrt(1 - h / height))`; times walking speed gives the reach.
- `climb_rope(c, px)`: hold up, tap jump (she grabs a rope over her by jumping with up held), keep up for
  `jump_peak_ms + px / climb_px_per_ms`. `climb_down(c, px)`: hold down `px / 0.165` ms.
- `pick_up(c, items)`: one press per item, `PICK_UP_GAP_MS` (260) apart. `stand_up`: tap the arrow she already faces.
- `attack`, `lucky_seven`: tap then `throw_gap` (set to clear `COMBAT.attack_lock_ms`). `drink_hp`, `drink_mp`: tap
  then 200 ms.

### RUN_JUMP_AFTER_MS = 150, and why

The game moves her in steps of about 30 ms. After three steps of the arrow she runs at 85% of walking speed: too fast
for the jump's kick (which takes her to full speed only from below 80%) and short of full speed herself, so a jump
keyed then leaves at 85% and lands short (a flat jump about 18 px short). In game on 2026-10-21, of 4 jumps keyed
120 ms after the arrow 3 left short, of 4 keyed at 100 ms 3 did, and none of the 10 keyed 130-160 ms did. gamelab's
movement engine fitted to those (`gamelab/motion/body.py`) says that from 150 ms at most 5% leave short
(`physics.BLIND_ENDS_MS`), so every running jump here goes at 150 ms or later.

### ACTIONS

`name -> (function, argument converters)`, trailing arguments optional where the function has a default. gamelab's
`do` command (`gamelab/__main__.py`) builds its choices from it and plays one move in the game, recorded; gamelab's
`control/timeline.action_events` turns a move into an exact key timeline.

modules.summary: Frozen dataclasses `Movement`, `Combat` and `Recovery` (instances `MOVEMENT`, `COMBAT`, `RECOVERY`) hold what was measured on 2026-10-18 with her thief at 1920x1080: walk speed, jump height and airtime, the attack lock, star flight. Plus her key bindings, monsters met, and comments on how the game behaves. gamelab imports `COMBAT` and `MOVEMENT` for its attack lock, tap-turn and release timing.
modules.details_md:
Measured 2026-10-18 on her rogue (level 19, claw, Lucky Seven level 4) on Victoria Road: Thicket Around the
Beach II, game window 1920x1080. Distances are game-window pixels; times are ms from key down. The docstring says to
re-measure with gamelab after gear, level, speed buffs or window size change.

### Movement (`MOVEMENT`)

| Field | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `reaction_ms` | 100 | key down → she visibly starts moving |
| `walk_px_per_ms` | 0.209 | ~209 px/s once moving |
| `walk_start_px` | 12 | holding an arrow t ms moves her ~12 + 0.209 t px (300 ms → 75 px, 1000 ms → 221 px) |
| `stop_slide_ms` | 200 | she keeps sliding this long after release |
| `tap_turn_ms` | 50 | a tap this short turns her without walking |
| `jump_airtime_ms` / `jump_peak_ms` | 530 / 260 | takeoff to landing / to the top |
| `jump_height_px` / `jump_length_px` | 104 / 120 | top of a jump; sideways distance of a running jump |
| `climb_px_per_ms` | 0.165 | rope/ladder, up or down (approximate) |

### Combat (`COMBAT`)

`attack_release_ms` 530 (the star leaves), `attack_lock_ms` 730 (presses before then are ignored, not queued, and
holding a key through the lock doesn't help), `melee_when_close` (a regular attack swipes the claw at a monster right
next to her), `hit_swallows_input` (while monsters keep hitting her, presses get lost: 4 Lucky Sevens used no MP),
Lucky Seven 8 MP at level 4, 2 stars, range 200 game units, a kill seen ~375 px away; a regular star flies 560 px
(400 map units) at 0.97 px/ms, hits seen up to 545 px and 60 map units above or below; a monster's touch knocks her
20-110 units.

### Recovery, bindings, monsters, notes

`RECOVERY`: chair and potion amounts from tooltips. `KEY_BINDINGS`: her Key Bindings window (preset 1) as read then.
`MONSTERS`: Snail, Slime, Pig with level, EXP per kill and how fighting them went. Comments record the Lie Detector
(the game's anti-bot check: a person must answer; gamelab stops all input, pages and shuts down), how to read the
screen, rope/loot/chair mechanics, platform rules (jump-through from below, down+jump drops through), and the map
scale: the screen draws the map 1.40625× (1080/768) at 1920x1080, and one minimap pixel is 11.4 map units.

### Where gamelab uses it

`control/actions.py` (attack lock + extra, `tap_turn_ms`, `stop_slide_ms`), `attack/stance.py` (`MOVEMENT`),
`behavior/fight.py` and `behavior/probe.py` (`attack_release_ms` for when a star is due), `sim/world.py`
(`ATTACK_LOCK = COMBAT.attack_lock_ms / 1000`).

modules.title: Key names
modules.tagline: config.toml key names to Windows virtual-key codes, with extended-key flags
modules.summary: `KEY_CODES` maps every name config.toml may use (letters, digits, f1-f12, arrows, modifiers, punctuation) to a Windows virtual-key code and whether it's an extended key. `parse` turns a name into a frozen `Key`; `Key.label` is how the coach writes it. gamelab's key player builds its list of pressable keys from `KEY_CODES`.
modules.details_md:
A *virtual-key code* (vk) is Windows' number for a key (0x41 for A, 0x25 for Left). An *extended* key is one
that sends an extra prefix byte on a real keyboard (arrows, Insert/Delete/Home/End/Page Up/Down, right Ctrl, right
Alt); `win32.send_key` sets `KEYEVENTF_EXTENDEDKEY` for those.

- Letters `a`-`z` and digits use their ASCII codes; `f1`-`f12` are `0x6F + n`.
- Modifiers use the **left/right-specific codes** (`shift` 0xA0, `rshift` 0xA1, `ctrl` 0xA2, `rctrl` 0xA3, `alt`
  0xA4, `ralt` 0xA5) because the low-level hook reports those, never the generic Shift/Ctrl/Alt codes.
- Punctuation: `` ` - = [ ] \ ; ' , . / `` plus space, enter, tab, esc, backspace, capslock, pause, scrolllock.

`parse(name)` strips and lower-cases, and raises `ValueError` listing every valid name for an unknown one (config.py
turns that into a `ConfigError` naming the setting). `name_of(vk)` goes back for logs (`vk_0x..` when unknown).
`Key.label` writes arrows as ← → ↑ ↓ and everything else upper-cased (`SHIFT`, `F4`), like a keycap on the overlay.

gamelab uses it everywhere keys are named: `control/player.py` (its `ALL_KEYS` from `KEY_CODES`), `control/keymap.py`
(reading the game's Key Bindings window), `control/timeline.py` (`SIM_KEYS`), `control/alarm.py` and the classes'
default bindings.

modules.title: Win32 calls (input, windows, timers)
modules.tagline: ctypes SendInput by scan code, tagged mouse input, the hook types, overlay styles
modules.summary: Every Windows call the helper needs, declared with ctypes and no third-party packages. `send_key` presses a key by scan code the way a keyboard does; `send_mouse_move` and `send_mouse_button` do the same for the mouse; every injected event carries `INJECTED_TAG`. gamelab's elevated key player presses all its keys and clicks through these functions.
modules.details_md:
### Keys: `send_key(key, down, tag=INJECTED_TAG)`

Builds one `INPUT` of type keyboard with `wVk = 0`, `wScan = scan_code(key)` (from `MapVirtualKeyW(vk,
MAPVK_VK_TO_VSC)`) and `KEYEVENTF_SCANCODE`, plus `KEYEVENTF_EXTENDEDKEY` for extended keys and `KEYEVENTF_KEYUP` for a
release, and sends it with `SendInput` (the Windows call that injects input events as if a device made them). **Scan codes, not virtual keys, because games read scan codes**: a scan code is the number the keyboard hardware sends for a physical key, a virtual-key code Windows' layout-dependent name for it. `dwExtraInfo`
carries the tag `0x4D484C50` ("MHLP") so the helper's own hook (`hook.py`) recognizes its own presses and doesn't
treat them as hers. A `SendInput` that doesn't insert 1 event raises the Windows error.

### Mouse

- `send_mouse_move(x, y)` moves the pointer as a mouse would: an absolute, virtual-desktop `MOUSEEVENTF_MOVE`
  event. `absolute(x, y, desk)` maps screen pixel x, y to SendInput's 0-65535 range across the virtual desktop
  (`GetSystemMetrics` 76-79), aiming at the pixel's middle. The docstring gives the reason: `SetCursorPos` moved the
  pointer but didn't carry an item dragged in the game's windows (2026-10-24).
- `send_mouse_button("lbutton" | "rbutton", down)` presses or releases where the pointer is.

### Hook plumbing, windows, timers

- `KBDLLHOOKSTRUCT`, `HOOKPROC`, `WH_KEYBOARD_LL`, `WM_KEYDOWN`... and the argtypes for `SetWindowsHookExW`,
  `CallNextHookEx`, `GetMessageW`, `PostThreadMessageW`, used by `hook.py`.
- `foreground_title()`: the focused window's title (the controller's focus check; gamelab's player refuses to press
  keys unless it's the game's).
- `make_click_through(tk_id)`: on the Tk window's real top-level (its parent) sets `WS_EX_LAYERED | TRANSPARENT |
  TOOLWINDOW | NOACTIVATE | TOPMOST`, so clicks pass through the coach and it never takes focus from the game.
- `enable_dpi_awareness()`: per-monitor DPI aware (`SetProcessDpiAwareness(2)`), so overlay coordinates are real pixels.
- `precise_timers()`: a context manager around `timeBeginPeriod(1)` / `timeEndPeriod(1)`, making sleeps accurate to
  ~1 ms instead of Windows' default ~15 ms. Key timing depends on it.

### Who else uses it

gamelab's `control/player.py` (`send_key`, `send_mouse_button`, `foreground_title`, `precise_timers`,
`enable_dpi_awareness`), `window.py` (`send_mouse_move`, `user32`, `kernel32`; `move_cursor` plays a `mouse_trail`
through it), `capture.py` (`enable_dpi_awareness`). `tests/conftest.py` replaces `send_key` and `foreground_title`

modules.title: Coach overlay
modules.tagline: A click-through panel at the top of the screen that narrates each step
modules.summary: `Coach` is a borderless, always-on-top, click-through Tk window that shows the running combo's title and current step in large text, then the whole recipe when it ends. `step`/`done`/`request_quit` are thread-safe (they only queue events); `run` owns the main thread.
modules.details_md:
### Look

A Tk root with no title bar (`overrideredirect`), topmost, dark background `#15171d`. Three labels: the title in
gold (`#ffc94d`, Segoe UI 13 bold, upper-cased), the step in white (Segoe UI 26 bold) and, at the end, the recipe
in pale blue (13). Text wraps at 60% of the screen width (`MAX_WIDTH`). The panel is centred horizontally,
`TOP_MARGIN` (60 px) from the top. `win32.make_click_through` gives it the layered, transparent, tool-window,
no-activate, topmost styles, so the mouse goes through it and it never steals focus from the game.

### Showing and hiding

Hidden means alpha 0; shown means alpha `VISIBLE_ALPHA` 0.96. It **must stay below 1.0**: at exactly 1.0 Tk drops the
layered window style that click-through needs.

### Threads

Calls arrive from the runner's thread (via the app's Narrator) and from the slow-mode toggle. `step` and `done` put a
tuple on a `SimpleQueue`; `_poll`, scheduled every `POLL_MS` (30 ms) on the Tk thread, drains it and calls `_show`.
`done` carries the recipe (steps joined by `  ·  `) and a linger time; `_poll` then schedules `_hide` after it
(a new show cancels a pending hide). `request_quit` only sets a flag (safe from the Ctrl+C signal handler); the next
`_poll` destroys the window, which ends `run`.

The module docstring's limit: it's visible over the game only in windowed or borderless-windowed mode, not
exclusive fullscreen.

modules.title: Human-like mouse trails
modules.tagline: Sigma-lognormal pointer paths with tremor and noise, sampled like a real mouse
modules.summary: `generate_trail(x1, y1, x2, y2)` returns rows of (t_ms, x, y): the mouse events a person's hand would make moving the pointer there. A primary stroke that undershoots a little plus up to 3 corrections, each with a lognormal speed profile along an arc, plus speed-scaled motor noise and 8-12 Hz tremor, polled at 125 Hz and reported only when the pixel changes. gamelab's `window.move_cursor` plays these trails.
modules.details_md:
### The model

The *sigma-lognormal* model (Plamondon's kinematic theory) describes a hand movement as overlapping strokes, each with a
lognormal speed profile: quick acceleration, long braking. Each `Stroke` has a time origin `t0`, `mu`, `sigma`, an
arc length and start/end directions; it bends along a circular arc. A stroke runs over its lognormal's
`mu ± SPAN_Z sigma` (`SPAN_Z` 3.5), its progress the lognormal's CDF cut to that span.

### Planning (`_plan`)

1. **Duration** from Fitts' law (movement time grows with the log of distance over target size): `natural_duration = 0.10 + 0.12 × log2(d / 20 + 1)` s for a 20 px target, times a
   lognormal(0, 0.10) person-to-moment spread.
2. **Primary stroke** over 0.85 of that, aimed off target: along the line by N(-4%, 5%) of the distance (primaries tend
   to undershoot), across by N(0, 2%). Bend N(0.18 sin(angle + 0.6), 0.08) rad (arm/wrist arcs), sigma U(0.22, 0.32).
3. **Corrections** until one lands exactly: each aims within N(0, 0.15 r) of the target unless the miss `r` is under
   half the target width or it's the `MAX_CORRECTIONS` (3rd) one, which lands exactly. It starts at the previous
   stroke's median time (`t0 + e^mu`) plus up to 25% of its duration, lasts (0.10 + 0.08 log2(r / 20 + 1)) × lognormal(0, 0.15) s,
   sigma U(0.25, 0.40), bend N(0, 0.25).

### Noise (`_Noise`)

On a 1 ms grid: an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck drift (a random wander that keeps being pulled back toward zero; tau 0.04 s) whose effect scales with the hand's speed
(`motor_noise` 0.04) and fades out as the last correction completes (it absorbs the drift), plus tremor: three
sinusoids at 8-12 Hz scaled to `tremor_px` (0.35 px) RMS, present only while the hand moves (enveloped by
speed / 20% of peak).

### Timing and sampling

Up to 8 times, `_last_change` finds when the rounded cursor last changes pixel (on a 0.5 ms grid) and every stroke is
re-scaled so that moment lands on the goal duration. With no `duration` the polling phase is random (the mouse isn't
synced to the hand) and the trail ends on the first poll after the cursor settles; with one, the last change is
re-timed onto it (in ~1% of trails, a slow 1-px flicker at the end, a few ticks earlier). Positions are sampled every
1/125 s, rounded to whole pixels, and a row is emitted only when the pixel changes; the last is forced onto the target.

### Use

gamelab's `window.move_cursor` gets the pointer's position, generates a trail and sends each row with
`win32.send_mouse_move` at its time, finishing with `SetCursorPos`. The elevated player plays it for the Lie
Detector's mouse mini-game (`lie_cursor` plans). CLI: `python mouse_trail.py 100 200 800 450 [--hz] [--duration] [--seed]`
prints CSV.

modules.title: config.toml loader
modules.tagline: Validates config.toml into frozen dataclasses: her keys, hotkeys, timing, stats, characters
modules.summary: `load`/`parse` read `config.toml` with tomllib into a frozen `Config`: her in-game key bindings (`GameKeys`), combo hotkeys, abort and slow-mode keys, `Timing`, her stats (`Character`) and other characters' tables (`CharacterConfig`). Every mistake becomes a `ConfigError` naming the setting. gamelab loads the same file through it, and uses `character()`/`characters()` to read just the stats early.
modules.details_md:
### The file's shape

The flat tables are the thief's: `[keys]` (her Key Config), `[hotkeys]` (combo name → button), `[control]` (`abort`,
default `esc`; `slow_mode`, default `f12`), `[timing]` (ms) and `[character]` (stats). Since 2026-10-27 other
characters (the magician) have tables of their own under `[characters.<id>]`, with `class`, the `name`/`job` lines
her bottom bar shows, and sub-tables `keys`, `timing`, `stats`, `skills`, `pet`, `buffs`. `game_window_title`
defaults to `"MapleStory"`. Top-level tables it doesn't know (config.toml's `[capture]`, `[perception]`) are left for
gamelab, which reads them itself.

### Validation (`parse`)

- `[keys]`: only `GameKeys` fields, and only the thief's class skills (a magician's skill in the flat `[keys]` is an
  error; `CLASS_SKILLS`). `left`, `right`, `jump`, `attack` are required; an empty string means "not bound / not
  learned yet" (field stays None). Each value goes through `keys.parse`.
- `[hotkeys]`: each name must be a combo (`combo_names`, from `COMBOS`).
- **Collisions** (`_check_collisions`): combo buttons and the slow-mode button are *swallowed* by the hook, so none may
  be one of her game keys, the abort key or each other. The abort key may share a game key (Esc still reaches the game).
- `[timing]`: known fields, whole ms ≥ 0. `[character]`: known fields, numbers > 0.
- Another character's sub-tables: `stats` are `Character` fields (not `lucky_seven`, the thief's skill level) above 0; `skills` her class's `CLASS_SKILL_LEVELS`, whole levels 0-30; `pet` the `PET_SETTINGS` (`hp_warning` / `mp_warning` a share of her bar below 1, `hp_heal` / `mp_heal` what a potion gives); `buffs` her class's `CLASS_BUFFS`, true or false.
- **`PERCEIVED`** (`hp`, `level`, `defence`) are refused in `[character]` and `[characters.<id>.stats]`: perception
  reads them (2026-10-28, the user: "I thought hp and level will come from perception, please remove them completely
  from config.toml"), after `hp = 774` at level 25 went stale while the HUD said 840 at level 28.
- `[characters]`: `default` (who plays when nothing names her; "thief" unless given; `"auto"` is refused as not built:
  it needs her bottom bar read). Ids match `[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}`; `class` is the id when the id is a class name.
  **A mistake in another character's table is kept with her** (`CharacterConfig.broken`), not raised, so the thief's
  commands and the key player never stop over it; mistakes in the thief's own table or in `default` are raised. Each
  other character's keys are also checked against the control keys.

### Her keys as the game has them (`followed`)

`followed(cfg, path)` returns `cfg` with `[keys]` replaced by the bindings in gamelab's `lab/keybindings-thief.json`
(written when gamelab reads the game's KEY BINDINGS window), plus a line saying which keys are in use. It keeps
`config.toml`'s keys when the file is missing, unreadable, marked `suspect` (doubted by a gamelab run and not
checked), names unknown actions or an unknown key, leaves an arrow/jump/attack unbound, or puts a game key on a combo button or the slow-mode key (`_check_collisions`). Only the helper app
calls it; gamelab has its own (`control/keymap.py`).

### Early readers for gamelab

`character(path)` returns just `[character]` (defaults if the file is missing) for gamelab's physics, which needs
her stats before anything else loads (the caller is `gamelab/character.py`'s `stats`/`load`, which `motion.physics`
asks); `characters(path)` returns `[characters]` (default and tables) for
`gamelab.character`. `Character`'s docstring holds the movement formula gamelab uses: walk 125 units/s × (SPEED + 20)/100
(Physics.img's walkSpeed and the client's hidden 20 Speed), jump 555 units/s × JUMP/100.

modules.title: OCR try-out CLI
modules.tagline: `python -m maplehelper.ocr hud|loot`: live or screenshot reads with timings
modules.summary: Reads the bottom bar or the pickup messages once a second from the game window (or from a screenshot) and prints what changed, with grab/OCR/CPU milliseconds. Its helpers keep the log quiet: a line that repeats rewrites itself, and a message seen on several reads is reported once.
modules.details_md:
### Options

`what` is `hud` or `loot` (a `regions.PRESETS` name). `--title` (default "MapleStory"), `--image FILE` (a screenshot of
the whole game window: black bars are trimmed with `content_box` and the preset region is cropped; `--as-is` if the
image is already the region), `--device cpu|cuda`, `--threads` (default 1; 0 = all cores), `--interval` (1 s),
`--once`, `--rows` (print the raw OCR lines), `--save DIR`.

### The loop

The models are loaded first (`engine.load()`), because onnxruntime prints load messages straight to the console and
would break a line being rewritten. Then each tick: grab the region with `capture.GameCapture` (or reuse the image),
read it (`OcrEngine.read` for the HUD with the preset's `min_height`; `LootReader.read` for loot), optionally save,
and report with `grab / ocr / cpu` timings. When the window can't be read, it says why ("not found", "minimized",
"covered", "off screen") and since when.

### Quiet output

- `Console`: a status line that only scrolls when the news changes. A repeat of the same key rewrites the line in
  place on a terminal (truncated to its width, since a wrapped line can't be rewritten); to a file, repeats are skipped.
- `HudReport`: a new line when HP, MP, EXP or level change (`parse_hud`), otherwise the time and timings refresh.
- `RowMemory`: the same line on screen read slightly differently ("PlayerOne", "PlayerOn") counts as seen if it's at
  the same height (within half a line) and `similar_text`; forgotten after `FORGET_S` (10 s).
- `LootReport`: each pickup message once when it shows up, compared with the previous read (a `Counter` of
  `(kind, amount, item, quantity)`), plus "skipping ... it stays put, so it's interface" when `StaticText` masks a line.
  Its docstring admits the limit: a line fading in and out of legibility can be listed twice.
- `Saver`: with `--save`, writes the crop as PNG plus a `.txt` of its OCR rows whenever a new line appears, at most
  `MAX_FILES` (200).

modules.title: Game window capture (for OCR)
modules.tagline: Finds the game window and grabs regions of its picture with mss, read-only
modules.summary: `GameCapture` finds the game's top-level window by title, follows it when it moves or closes, trims the black bars the game adds, and grabs a region's pixels (BGR numpy) with mss. It refuses to grab when the window is missing, minimized, covered by another app, or partly off screen, and says which in `problem`.
modules.details_md:
Read-only, like any screenshot tool: the window is found by title, pixels come from a screen grab, and the game's
process is never opened, read or sent input. Used by the OCR CLI; gamelab has its own capture (`gamelab/capture.py`,
DXGI or mss, and the perception service's frames).

### Finding the window (`find_window`)

`EnumWindows` over visible windows, skipping this process's own windows, its console and classes in
`NOT_GAME_CLASSES` (`Chrome_WidgetWin_0/1`, `MozillaWindowClass`, `ApplicationFrameWindow`, the console and
Windows Terminal classes, Explorer's `CabinetWClass`, Notepad, Notepad++),
because their titles may mention the game. An exact (case-insensitive) title match wins over one that merely
contains it.

### Where the picture is

- `client_box(hwnd)`: the client area (no title bar or borders) in screen pixels; None if gone or minimized.
- `play_area()`: that minus the black bars. Bars are measured with `regions.content_box` on a grab of the whole
  client, again whenever the client size changes and every `BARS_EVERY_S` (30 s), but only when the whole client is
  on screen and uncovered (an edge cut off by the monitor would look like a bar).
- `visible_part(box, monitors, slack)`: the part on the monitor showing most of it; None when more than `slack`
  (`OFF_SCREEN_SLACK`, 10 px) hangs off (a grab gives black there).
- `covered(hwnd, box)`: samples 5 points (centre and 10%/90% near each corner) with `WindowFromPoint` → root
  ancestor. Another app's window there means covered; this process's windows and click-through windows
  (`WS_EX_TRANSPARENT`, like the coach overlay) don't count. A screen grab takes whatever is on top, so a covered
  region must not be read.

### Grabbing

`grab(region)` = `play_area` → region box → `_visible` → `covered` check → `mss.grab` → BGR array (alpha dropped).
`set_dpi_aware()` (per-monitor v2) makes window rectangles physical pixels, the same as mss's, so crops line up on
scaled displays. `mss` is imported inside `__init__` so `regions` and `parse` stay usable without it. Use it from one
thread.

modules.title: OCR engine (shared RapidOCR)
modules.tagline: One shared RapidOCR engine per settings, tuned to stay light while the game runs
modules.summary: `OcrEngine` wraps RapidOCR (text detection + recognition models on ONNX Runtime), loads its models once, serializes reads with a lock, and returns `Row`s (text, confidence, box) in reading order in the input image's pixels. `shared(settings)` hands every reader the same engine. gamelab's perception and pet feeder read text through it.
modules.details_md:
### Defaults that keep it off the game's CPU (module docstring)

- **One ONNX Runtime thread.** The library's default uses every core: on a 12-core / 24-thread CPU a read finished
  ~3× sooner but kept ~16 cores busy (2 s of CPU per read instead of 0.4 s).
- **Detector only shrinks** (`limit_type` "max", 960 px). RapidOCR's default ("min") enlarges small crops before
  detecting, which costs more than it gains on game text.
- **No text-direction classifier** (`use_cls` False): game text is never upside down, and the classifier flips some lines.
- On an NVIDIA GPU (`device="cuda"`) a small crop reads in ~35 ms with about one core busy. cuDNN's convolution search
  is set to HEURISTIC, because the default (EXHAUSTIVE) re-tunes kernels for every new text-line width.

### Reading

`read(image, min_height=0)` under the lock: load if needed, `upscale` the image (Lanczos, same aspect) to at least
`min_height` px tall when it's shorter (small game text reads better bigger), run RapidOCR, and convert with
`rows_from`: each box's 4 corners become a `Row` (centre x/y, height, left, right) divided back by the upscale
factor; rows are grouped into lines (same line when centres are within half the taller box's height), lines top to
bottom, boxes left to right. Returns None when OCR can't load (logged once).

### Loading

`_load` imports `rapidocr` late (the package stays importable without it), builds `RapidOCR(params=...)`, and loads the
detection and recognition models right away through RapidOCR's private loaders (skipped if they're gone), because
RapidOCR otherwise loads the text model only once something is detected. With CUDA, `_add_conda_dll_dir` puts the
env's `Library\bin` on PATH (conda does so only when the env is activated; onnxruntime finds the CUDA DLLs through
PATH). `_check_providers` warns when CUDA was asked for but a model runs elsewhere (RapidOCR falls back to the CPU
with only a log line). `load()` loads up front so onnxruntime's console output happens at a known time.

modules.title: Loot box reader
modules.tagline: OCR of the pickup-message box that learns to ignore interface text sitting in it
modules.summary: `LootReader.read` OCRs the loot box, keeps the rows that parse as pickup messages, and teaches `StaticText` which other text stays put (a party panel's names, say). Text that doesn't parse and stays in place for 15 s is painted out before OCR, so it's neither detected nor read again; every 30 s one read goes unmasked to free spots whose text is gone.
modules.details_md:
### The problem

The loot box is a fixed part of the screen, so other interface can sit in it (the party panel's member names with HP
bars, for one). Pickup messages scroll up as new ones arrive and fade within ~12 s; interface text stays where it is.

### StaticText

Each read's *ignored* rows (rows that didn't parse as a pickup) feed `learn`:
- Rows that look like part of a pickup message (`_PICKUP_WORDS`: received, gained, earned variants, EXP, mesos, "(+")
  are never interface: a message read only in part while fading.
- Each row is matched to a known *spot* by `same_line` against the spot's **anchor** (where the text first showed, so
  a message scrolling up doesn't count as staying put), or becomes a new spot.
- A spot seen for `STATIC_S` (15 s, longer than any message stays) becomes **masked**.
- An unmasked spot not seen for `FORGET_S` (3 s) is dropped. On a recheck read, a masked spot with no text on or near it
  (`_near`: overlapping or within a line height) is freed: the interface is gone (she left the party, closed a window).

`prepare` paints each masked spot (plus `PAD` 4 px) with `_surround`: the median colour of a 3 px ring just outside the
box. Not black, because a black patch on a grey panel has corners OCR reads as characters. Every `RECHECK_S` (30 s,
counted from the first blackout) one read goes without the mask.

### Matching helpers

- `similar_text(a, b, ratio=0.6)`: compares letters and digits only; one inside the other, or a difflib ratio ≥ 0.6.
  OCR drops or swaps a character or two between reads ("PlayerOne", "PlayerOn", "* PlayerOne").
- `same_line(a, b)`: centres within half the taller row's height, overlapping left to right, similar text.

### LootReader

`read(crop, now)`: `static.prepare` → `engine.read(image, min_height=preset.min_height)` (the LOOT preset enlarges to
450 px tall) → `parse_loot(row.text, item_names)` per row → `static.learn(ignored, ...)` → `LootRead(rows, messages,
ignored, interface, recheck)`. Item names default to `ITEM_NAMES`, which also completes names the game cut off with "...".

modules.title: Text to game values (HUD and pickups)
modules.tagline: Parses OCR'd HP/MP/EXP/level and pickup lines, tolerant of OCR's misreads
modules.summary: `parse_hud` pulls HP, MP, EXP points and percent and her level from the bottom bar's lines, working the level out from the EXP table because the level digits misread. `parse_loot` turns one line into an item (name, quantity), EXP or mesos `LootLine`, completing cut-off item names with `match_prefix`. Doubtful reads are marked unsure. gamelab's looting uses `parse_loot` and `match_prefix`.
modules.details_md:
OCR on game fonts confuses a few characters often enough to plan for: "+" read as "t", "4", "-" or "=", "1" as
"l", "I", "i", "L" or "|", "0" as "O" or "o", "m" as "rn", "..." as ".", and accents added. Numbers are folded back
where a number is expected (`_DIGIT_FIX`, only the unambiguous ones: folding S or B too would turn a label stuck to a
number into digits), and a value read from a doubtful character is marked unsure.

### The bottom bar (`parse_hud`)

Rows are joined into one text. `HP`/`MP` patterns read `cur / max` (`_pair`): the bar writes `HP[642/642]` and OCR reads
the closing `]` as `1` often enough (`HP[642/6421`), so with an opening `[` and no closing bracket a trailing 1-like
character is dropped; a pair with `cur > max` is discarded. `EXP 1234 [12.34%]` gives points and percent. No HP and
no EXP → None (not the bar).

**Level**: first from EXP (`level_from_exp`): `needed = points × 100 / percent` must be within `LEVEL_TOLERANCE` (2%)
of exactly one level's requirement, and only when `percent ≥ MIN_PERCENT` (1.0; below it the two decimals are too
coarse). Else from the digits ("LV. 19", or a lone 1-3 digit row left of the gauges), repaired because the stylized 1
reads as 0 ("19" as "09"): try "1" + rest, then the digits without leading zeros; a candidate is kept only if the EXP
fits it (`_exp_fits`: its requirement holds the points and, with a percentage, points/percent lands within
(0.02 + 0.01/percent) of it). `level_source` says "exp" or "read".

### Pickup lines (`parse_loot`)

Text is unaccented and whitespace-collapsed. Three kinds:
- **Item**: `<name> x<n> earned` with OCR's many "earned" spellings, the "x" possibly lost after a cut name's "..."
  ("Orange Mushroo...51"). A name ending in "..."-like punctuation is **cut**. With names given, a cut name is
  completed with `match_prefix`; a full name is matched with `match_name`, then `match_prefix` (it may have lost its
  "..."). `sure` when the quantity's characters were real digits.
- **EXP**: an amount `(+21)` and "EXP" with a "received"-like word.
- **Mesos**: an amount and a mesos-like word (regex, or a 4-7 letter word within difflib 0.7 of "mesos": resos, mesps,
  mcsos) with "gain"/"have" or "meso". For EXP and mesos, `sure` needs a real "+" and a closing bracket.

### Names

- `match_name`: an exact match of the lower-cased form, else difflib scores against plain and *folded* forms (0→o,
  1→l, |→l, 5→s, rn→m, punctuation dropped). The best must score ≥ `NAME_MIN` (0.8) and beat the runner-up by
  `NAME_MARGIN` (0.07). The forms are cached per name list (`_forms`, lru_cache).
- `match_prefix`: for a cut name of at least `PREFIX_MIN` (6) folded characters, the one longer name starting with it;
  only if none starts with it exactly, names whose start is within `PREFIX_EDITS` (20%) edits of it (`_start_edits`,
  an edit distance anchored at the start: "Snail Shell" isn't the start of "Red Snail Shell"). Several fits → None.

modules.tagline: Where the game draws HUD and pickup text, as fractions of its picture
modules.summary: A `Region` is a box as fractions (0..1) of the game picture, so it fits any window size because the game's interface scales with its window. Two presets: `HUD` (the bottom 6%) and `LOOT` (bottom right, enlarged to 450 px before OCR). `content_box` trims the black bars a game adds to keep its aspect ratio.
modules.details_md:
### Regions and presets

`Region(left, top, right, bottom)` validates `0 ≤ left < right ≤ 1` and the same for top/bottom. `box(area)` gives the
region in pixels of an area (x, y, w, h), at least 1×1; `crop(picture)` cuts it out of a whole picture.

A `Preset` is a name, a region and `min_height` (crops shorter than this are enlarged before OCR; 0 = never).
- `HUD = Preset("hud", Region(0.0, 0.94, 1.0, 1.0), min_height=0)`: the bottom bar (level, job, name, HP, MP, EXP);
  its text is big enough as is.
- `LOOT = Preset("loot", Region(0.78, 0.57, 1.0, 0.86), min_height=450)`: the pickup messages stacked bottom right of
  the play area, above the skill bar and below the chat bubbles; small text, enlarged to 450 px tall.

The docstring: the presets are layout measurements of MapleStory Classic World published with Maple Helper, measured
at 1368x800, 1922x1112 and 2734x1568.

### Black bars (`content_box`)

The part of a picture without the bars a game adds to keep its aspect (16:9 on an ultrawide, 4:3 on 16:9). For
columns and rows, `_trim` takes each one's brightest value; content starts at the first value above `_DARK` (12).
Only real bars count: at least `_MIN_BAR` (4) px, the two sides within `_BAR_SLACK` (2) px of each other, and leaving
a picture of a shape the game draws (`GAME_ASPECTS` 16:9, 16:10, 4:3, within 2%). A dark scene touching one edge, or
black beyond the ends of a map narrower than the window (the interface still spans it), is left alone.

modules.title: .wz package reader
modules.tagline: Parses Wizet PKG1 packages: directory, client-version offsets, property trees
modules.summary: `Package` opens a `.wz` file (memory-mapped), lists its images and parses one into a property tree of dicts, numbers, strings, `Canvas` pictures (pixels left unread), `Vector`s and `Uol` links. Directory offsets are scrambled with a hash of the client version, which isn't stored, so it tries versions until every offset lands on an image. `Reader` also parses the images decrypted out of .ms packs.
modules.details_md:
### The format

The client splits each category into packages: `X.wz` (an index), `X_000.wz` (the data) and `_Canvas/` (its pictures).
A package holds folders and *images*; an image is a tree of properties: numbers, text, pictures (canvases), vectors,
links to other properties, and sub-trees. Classic World only XOR-masks the text (no AES), so no key is needed.

### Reading an image (`Reader`)

- `_cint` / `_clong`: a "compressed" int: one signed byte, or -128 followed by 4 (or 8) bytes.
- `_string`: a signed length byte (negative = one byte a character, positive = UTF-16; -128/127 = a 4-byte length
  follows); each character is XORed with a mask counting up from 0xAA (0xAAAA for UTF-16).
- `_block` / `_typename`: a name or text stored inline (tags 0x00/0x73) or at an offset from the image start
  (0x01/0x1B), which is how repeated strings are shared.
- `_properties`: a count, then per property a name and a type byte: 0 null, 2/11 int16, 3/19 compressed int, 20
  compressed long, 4 float (0x80 then the float, else 0), 5 double, 8 string, 9 an *extended* value prefixed by its
  length (so unknown kinds can be skipped).
- `_extended`: `Property` (a sub-tree), `Canvas` (optional properties, then width, height, format; the pixel bytes'
  position is kept in `raw` for `canvas.pixels`), `Shape2D#Vector2D`, `Shape2D#Convex2D` (a list of vectors), `UOL`;
  anything else (sounds, the embedded font) becomes the string `"<typename>"`.

### The directory (`Package`)

The file starts with `PKG1`; byte 12 holds the offset of the data start, where a 16-bit field holds the version check (an 8-bit value: only that check of the version is stored, not the version). `_listing` reads a
folder's entries (kind 3 folder, 4 image; kind 2 means the name is stored elsewhere) with their size and *where* their
scrambled offset is. The real offset is `((scramble(p, h) ^ stored) + 2 × start)`, where `scramble` mixes the
position, the version hash `h`, `OFFSET_KEY` (0x581C3F6D) and a rotate by the low 5 bits.

`_resolve` tries client versions 1 to `MAX_VERSION` (10,000): `version_hash` (h = 32h + ord(c) + 1 over the decimal
digits) must give the stored 8-bit check (`version_check_of`, the XOR of its bytes with 0xFF); then `_walk` must
place every offset inside the file and every image's first byte must be 0x73. The first version that passes is kept
in `Package.version`.

`jsonable` turns a tree into plain JSON: canvases as `{"_canvas": [w, h, format], ...props}`, vectors as
`{"_vec": [x, y]}`, links as `{"_uol": path}`. gamelab's `localization/mapdata.py` uses `Package` and `jsonable`
directly to read map images and `Map/Map_000.wz` `Physics.img`.

modules.title: .ms pack reader (ChaCha20)
modules.tagline: Decrypts the newer .ms packs that hold Mob and Skill data
modules.summary: Newer clients keep some categories in `Data/Packs/*.ms`; Classic World does so for Mob and Skill. A pack is ChaCha20-encrypted with keys derived from its file name and a salt stored in it; only the first 1 KB of each image is encrypted, and inside is an ordinary .wz image. `MsPack` lists and decrypts images and parses them with `wz.Reader`. The format follows WzComparerR2's reader (MIT).
modules.details_md:
*ChaCha20* is a standard stream cipher: from a 32-byte key, a 12-byte nonce and a block counter it makes a stream of pseudo-random bytes that is XORed with the data.

### Layout and keys

1. **Filler and salt.** The file starts with random filler whose length is `sum(ord(c) for c in name) % 312 + 30`
   (from the lower-cased file name). Each filler byte, halved as a signed value, masks what follows: the version byte
   (must decode to `VERSION` 4, else the pack is refused), the salt's length, and the salt's UTF-16 characters
   (each decoded with `((a | 0x4B) << 1) - a - 75`).
2. **Header.** 8 bytes decrypted with ChaCha20 under `header_key(name + salt)` (each key byte: a character of
   name+salt plus its index, XOR `KEY_OBSCURE`) give a hash and the image count; the hash must equal the sum of the
   masked salt-length word, the masked version, the version, the count and the salt's raw 16-bit units, or the
   file name is wrong.
3. **Image table** at `p + 8 + (sum(3 × ord(c)) % 212) + 64`, decrypted under `table_key(name + salt)` by
   `TableReader`: the game decrypts it in 64-byte blocks **whose block counter goes back to 0 whenever a read ends
   exactly at a block's end**. The format depends on that quirk. Each row: the image path (UTF-16), seven int32s
   (checksum, flags, start, size, aligned, two unknown), a 16-byte entry key and two more int32s.
4. **Images** start at the next whole KB after the table; an image's start is `data_start + start × 1024`.

### Decrypting an image (`image_bytes`)

`image_cipher(salt, path, entry_key)` derives the image's own key, nonce and first block counter: an FNV-1a hash of
the salt (0x811C9DC5, ×0x1000193), its decimal digits, the path's characters and the entry key, XOR `KEY_OBSCURE`;
the nonce is 4 zero bytes plus 8 bytes of a mixed hash, and the counter the last 4. Only `min(size, 1024)` bytes are
XORed with the keystream; the rest is plain. `image(path)` parses the result with `wz.Reader(...).tree()`.

### ChaCha20

`chacha20(key, nonce, counter, blocks)` is a numpy implementation of RFC 7539 (20 rounds, 64-byte blocks), computing
many blocks at once as columns. One deviation is deliberate: the block counter carries into the nonce's first word
(`state[13]`), "as the game's does". The tests check it against RFC 7539's test vector.

modules.title: Pictures and monster frames
modules.tagline: Decodes canvases to RGBA and finds monster frames, item icons, HUD glyphs, minimap markers
modules.summary: `pixels(canvas)` inflates and decodes a picture (BGRA4444, BGRA8888, RGB565) to an RGBA array. The other functions know where newer clients keep the actual pixels (separate `_Canvas` packages, `_inlink` and `_outlink` references) and return what gamelab's perception matches against: a monster's animation frames with origin and body box, item icons, meso coins, the status bar's digits, the minimap's markers.
modules.details_md:
### Decoding (`pixels`)

After a canvas's size and format come a second format byte, 4 zero bytes, the data length (int32, counting one more
zero byte), that byte, then zlib-compressed pixels. The game's streams end without zlib's end marker, so they're
inflated with a `decompressobj` rather than `zlib.decompress`. Formats (the canvas's format plus the second byte):
`1` BGRA4444 (each 4-bit channel × 17), `2` BGRA8888, `513` RGB565, `517` RGB565 with one value per 16×16 block
(backgrounds' plain fills, as MapleLib reads it). Anything else raises (DXT-compressed pictures aren't decoded yet).

### Where the pixels are

Newer clients keep pictures out of the data images:
- **Monsters**: the frames in `Packs/Mob_00000.ms` are empty canvases with a `_hash`; the pixels are at the same path
  ("stand/0") in the monster's image in `Mob/_Canvas/_Canvas_000.wz`. A frame that repeats another says so with
  `_inlink` ("move/2"). `mob_frames(mob_id, actions=("stand", "move", "hit1"))` returns one record per distinct
  picture: action, index, RGBA, `origin` (the point at the monster's feet), body box corners `lt`/`rb`, `head`
  (map units, y negative upward), `delay` (ms; some monsters store it as text). The pictures face left.
- **Items**: `Item/<Consume|Etc>/<....>.img` holds 1×1 placeholders; `item_icon(id)` reads `iconRaw` (the icon as it
  lies on the ground, without its inventory shadow) from the folder's `_Canvas/_Canvas_000.wz` (`ITEM_FOLDERS`:
  id // 1,000,000 → 2 Consume, 4 Etc). `item_ids_beside` lists the items kept in the same image (the ores, the potions).
- **Mesos**: `meso_frames()`: the spinning frames of the 4 kinds of coins/bills/sacks in `Item/Special` 0900.img.
- **UI**: placeholders whose `_outlink` names a path from the copy's root ("UI/_Canvas/Basic.img/BtOK2/normal/0").

- `status_numbers()`: the status bar's 7 px number glyphs (digits, `,`, `.`, `%`, slash, brackets); `level_numbers()`:
  its 11×13 orange level digits; `status_panel()`: the 570×64 panel behind level, job and name with its origin.
- `minimap_markers()`: the minimap's markers (her, other players, party, NPC, portal...) with their origins.
- `export_pictures(tree, dest)`: every picture of an image tree as PNG at its path, plus `tree.json` naming each file.

The packages are opened once and cached (`lru_cache` on `_mob_pack`, `_mob_canvases`, `_item_canvases`, `_image`).

`perception/loot.py` (`item_icon`, `item_ids_beside`, `meso_frames`), `perception/exp_number.py` (`status_numbers`,
`level_numbers`, `status_panel`), `perception/keybindings.py`, `misses.py`, `touches.py`, `stat_window.py` (`pixels`,
`source`), `localization/mapdata.py` and `mapart.py` (map art, the minimap picture, `_mob_pack`), `sim/world.py`.

Each table is a function of parsed trees, so the tests can feed it small hand-made trees without the game's files;

|---|---|---|

flows.title: A combo button becomes timed keys
flows.summary: She presses F4 in the game; the helper hides it, plays the Jump-Back Shot on its own thread and narrates each step.
flows.trigger: A real key press while `python -m maplehelper` runs

steps.text: Windows calls the low-level hook on the keyboard-hook thread. Events tagged INJECTED_TAG (the helper's own) are skipped; the rest go to on_key.
The focused title contains "MapleStory" and F4 is a hotkey: the key is swallowed (and its key-up later), and the runner is asked to start jump_back_shot.
Idle: STARTED and queued for the runner thread. Busy: QUEUED if the running combo ends within 300 ms (newest press wins), else DROPPED.
On the combo-runner thread: both arrows released, the combo timed by a dry run (sets the expected end), a Ctx built with front/back from her facing.
Holds the away arrow 100 ms, jumps, keeps pushing 60 ms, releases, holds the front arrow 50 ms and through the air throw, then waits 750 ms. Each say shows a step.
Every down/up is one SendInput keyboard event by scan code, tagged 0x4D484C50.
The Tk thread drains the event queue every 30 ms and shows each step; at the end the recipe stays 3000 ms.

When the combo ends, `finally` has released every held key and shown the recipe; a press buffered in its last 300 ms starts next (abort flag cleared under the lock). Esc stops the combo mid-wait and also forgets any buffered press, so the runner goes idle.

flows.title: gamelab turns the helper's combos and moves into key timelines
flows.summary: The same combo and move scripts run on a virtual clock in gamelab, giving exact [ms, key, down/up] timelines for tests and the key player.
flows.trigger: A gamelab command or test that plays a combo (`gamelab combo ...`) or a move (`gamelab do ...`)

steps.text: gamelab's timeline.her_setup loads config.toml with the combo names, for her keys and timing (her keys then follow the game's Key Bindings as gamelab remembered them).
Builds _Clock, a Ctx subclass whose sender records [round(now), key name, down/up] and whose wait advances a virtual clock; records both arrows up first, as the runner does.
The combo's script runs unchanged against the clock; Ctx.release_all closes any held key.
For `gamelab do walk left 150`, the move's function and converters come from ACTIONS; timeline.action_events records it the same way.
The elevated key player (gamelab/control/player.py) presses the timeline's keys with send_key while the game is in front.

flows.title: A pickup message is read off the screen
flows.summary: The loot box is cropped, known interface text painted out, OCR'd, and each line parsed into an item, EXP or mesos gain.
flows.trigger: `python -m maplehelper.ocr loot`, or gamelab's eyes reading the pickup log

steps.text: Finds the game window, trims black bars, checks it isn't covered or off screen, and grabs the LOOT region (x 78-100%, y 57-86% of the picture). gamelab crops the same region from its own frames.
Paints out text known to be interface with the median colour around it, except on the unmasked recheck every 30 s.
Enlarges the crop to 450 px tall when it's shorter, runs RapidOCR (one CPU thread by default) and returns Rows in reading order in the crop's pixels.
Each row becomes an item (name, quantity), EXP or mesos LootLine through regexes tolerant of OCR's misreads; doubtful reads are sure=False.
A name the game cut off with "..." is completed to the one known item name it starts (ITEM_NAMES), or kept marked cut.
Rows that aren't pickups and stay in place 15 s are masked from then on; spots whose text is gone are freed on a recheck.

flows.title: From the game folder to tables and map data
flows.summary: The game's Data folder is copied once, then its packages are opened, decrypted where needed, parsed into trees and summarized; gamelab reads the same trees for its maps.
flows.trigger: `python -m gamedata copy --install <game folder>`, then `python -m gamedata tables` (or a gamelab map load)

steps.text: Copies <install>/appdata/Data into gamedata/data/copy, skipping Sound and files whose size and time already match.
Opens a PKG1 package, reads its directory and tries client versions until every scrambled offset lands on an image.
For Packs/Mob and Skill: decodes the salt, checks the header, decrypts the image table with ChaCha20 (counter-reset quirk) and each image's first 1 KB.
Parses an image into a tree of numbers, unmasked strings, Canvas pictures (pixels left for later), vectors and links.
Summarizes items, mobs, maps, skills, Physics.img and body animation delays; the CLI writes each to gamedata/data/out/tables/<name>.json.
gamelab's map model reads the map's image and Physics.img with the same Package and jsonable (monster facts from the Mob pack), caching the parsed map as JSON under gamedata/data/out/maps.

not_done: maplehelper's README still lists "Tested only against the key viewer, not against MapleStory itself" as a known limit, though the combos' timing was measured in game on 2026-10-18 and gamelab's `combo` command plays them there.
actions.jump_to_ledge is not confirmed in game: two attempts at ~90 px ledges with ~60 px gaps both fell short; ropes are the sure way up.
game.py's pixel numbers were measured at a 1920x1080 window on one map and one character level; the docstring says to re-measure after gear, level, speed buffs or window size change.
config [characters] default = "auto" (the profile whose name her bottom bar shows) is refused: reading her bottom bar isn't built yet.
Character.avoid and mp_regen: the comment says nothing reads them yet (each gamelab module keeps its own copy, the thief's).
The OCR CLI's LootReport compares with the previous read only, so a message fading in and out can be listed twice; counting each pickup exactly once needs a tracker following the message stack.
item_names covers Victoria Island only (Orbis, Ossyria and El Nath content left out).
gamedata: DXT-compressed pictures aren't decoded; sounds and the embedded font are listed but not decoded; only .ms version 4 is supported.
Not in the game's data files at all (gamedata README): chat and pickup message templates, the EXP table, damage and attack-speed formulas, drop tables.
Some skill animations have negative frame delays; what the sign means isn't known (tables.actions).
The sound Lie Detector (four numbers read aloud) is in UI.wz but hasn't been seen in game yet (gamedata README).
